train.content: When is a graph database used?

Graph databases are used when relationships between data are very important. Node and edge structure. In SQL, JOINs slow down as they deepen; in graph DBs, relationship traversal is natural and fast. Use cases: social networks (friend relationships), recommendation engines (similar products), knowledge graphs (Google uses them), fraud detection, network topology. Neo4j is the most popular graph database with Cypher query language. Amazon Neptune, ArangoDB are alternatives. Not suitable for every data model — SQL is better for simple CRUD apps. Very powerful for relationship-heavy data.

train.content: What is a PWA (Progressive Web App)?

A PWA delivers native app experience using web technologies (HTML, CSS, JS). Can work offline (with Service Worker), send push notifications, be added to home screen, load quickly. No App Store needed — accessed via URL. Advantages: single codebase for all platforms, automatic updates, SEO benefit. Disadvantages: limited access to some native APIs (especially on iOS), push notifications on iOS only recently supported. Twitter Lite, Starbucks, Pinterest use PWAs. For small-medium projects, a PWA can be considered instead of a native app.

train.content: What's the difference between containers and VMs?

Virtual Machine (VM): runs a full operating system on a hypervisor (VMware, VirtualBox). Heavy (GB-sized), slow startup (minutes), full isolation. Container (Docker): shares host OS kernel, only packages the application and its dependencies. Light (MB-sized), fast startup (seconds), sufficient isolation. Why containers won: compatible with microservice architecture, fast in CI/CD, dev-production consistency. When VMs: different OS needed, strong isolation required, legacy applications. In practice they're used together — containers run on VMs. Kubernetes orchestrates containers.

train.content: How to ensure security in software projects?

Security should be considered at every stage of software — 'security by design'. Core principles: input validation (never trust user input), parameterized queries (prevent SQL injection), output encoding (prevent XSS), HTTPS mandatory, distinguish authentication from authorization, least privilege principle, dependency updates (npm audit, pip audit), secret management (environment variables, vault — never leave passwords in code), rate limiting, correct CORS configuration. Know the OWASP Top 10 list. Security testing: SAST (static analysis), DAST (dynamic analysis), penetration testing. Finding vulnerabilities is easy, fixing them is hard — write securely from the start.

train.content: How does DNS work?

DNS (Domain Name System) translates domain names to IP addresses — the phonebook of the internet. When you type google.com you're actually going to an IP like 142.250.80.14. Steps: browser checks DNS cache → OS cache → ISP DNS → Root DNS server → TLD (.com) server → Authoritative DNS server. DNS record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT (verification). DNS propagation — changes can take 24-48 hours to spread. Cloudflare DNS (1.1.1.1), Google DNS (8.8.8.8) are fast alternatives. DNS security: DNSSEC, DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH). Every web developer needs to understand DNS.

train.content: What do open-source licenses mean?

Open-source licenses determine how your code can be used. MIT: most permissive — use, modify, distribute, commercial use, just keep the license. Apache 2.0: MIT-like but adds patent protection. GPL: modifications must also be open source (copyleft) — commercial use exists but you must share source code. BSD: very similar to MIT. LGPL: for libraries — code using the library can be closed source but library changes must be open. ISC: simplified version of MIT. Unlicensed code: copyright applies by default — others can't use it. Don't forget to add a license to your projects.

train.content: What is WebRTC?

WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication) enables direct audio, video, and data communication between browsers. Establishes peer-to-peer connections without going through a server — low latency. Zoom, Google Meet, Discord use this. Core components: getUserMedia (camera/microphone access), RTCPeerConnection (connection), RTCDataChannel (data transfer). STUN/TURN servers help devices behind NAT connect. A signaling server (using WebSocket) establishes the initial connection, then communication is direct. The foundational technology for video conferencing, screen sharing, and file transfer applications.

train.content: What do HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 bring?

HTTP/1.1 opens separate connections for each request — slow. HTTP/2: multiplexing (multiple requests over single connection), header compression (HPACK), server push (sends resources before client asks), binary protocol. HTTP/3: runs on QUIC protocol (UDP-based — faster than TCP), fewer handshakes, connection migration (connection doesn't drop when switching from WiFi to 4G). Google, YouTube, Facebook use HTTP/3. Most modern web servers and CDNs support HTTP/2. Nginx and Cloudflare support HTTP/3. HTTP/2 should be the minimum for web performance. Protocol version visible in browser DevTools.

train.content: What does webhook mean?

A webhook is a mechanism that automatically sends an HTTP request to a specified URL when an event occurs. The opposite of polling — instead of constantly asking 'did something happen?', it notifies you when something does. Examples: send Slack notification when a GitHub PR is created, update database when Stripe receives payment, send email when a form is filled. A webhook URL is an endpoint — it processes incoming POST requests. Security: signature verification with webhook secret. Retry mechanism: retries on failure. One of the cornerstones of event-driven architecture. Zapier and IFTTT work on webhooks.

train.content: What does event sourcing mean?

Event sourcing is the approach of storing all events rather than current state in the database. Traditional: user balance is $1000. Event sourcing: deposited +$500, spent -$200, received transfer +$700. Each event is immutable — can't be changed, only new events are added. Advantages: complete history, audit trail, ability to reconstruct state at any point in time. Used together with CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation). Kafka or EventStore tools. Used in banking, e-commerce, and gaming. Complex but very powerful in certain domains.

train.content: How to stay productive while studying for exams?

Productivity during exam prep is crucial. Pomodoro technique: 25 minutes focused study, 5 minute break, repeat. After 4 cycles take a longer break. Active recall: test yourself instead of re-reading notes. Spaced repetition: review material at increasing intervals. Study environment: dedicated quiet space, phone in another room. Sleep: 7-8 hours minimum, learning consolidates during sleep. Exercise: 30 minutes daily improves concentration. Nutrition: avoid sugar crashes, eat brain food (nuts, fruits). Track progress: what you studied each day. Study groups: for difficult topics, teaching others helps. Don't compare with others — focus on your own progress.

train.content: Why is web accessibility important?

Accessibility (a11y) means websites and applications can be used by people with disabilities. Visually impaired: screen reader compatibility (alt text, ARIA labels, heading structure). Hearing impaired: video captions. Motor impaired: keyboard navigation, large clickable areas. Cognitive: simple language, consistent navigation. WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the standard. May be legally required — ADA (US), EAA (EU). 15-20% of the population has some form of disability — that's a large user base. Use semantic HTML, check color contrast, ensure proper tab order. Check Lighthouse accessibility score.

train.content: How does JWT (JSON Web Token) work?

JWT is a token standard used for authentication. Consists of three parts: Header (algorithm and type), Payload (user info — id, role, expiry), Signature (verification). Encoded with Base64, separated by dots. Flow: user logs in → server creates JWT → client sends it in header with each request (Bearer token) → server verifies signature. Advantage over sessions: no need to store state on server (stateless), easy in microservices. Disadvantage: if token is stolen the session is compromised, token size is larger than cookies. Refresh tokens manage expiration. passport-jwt, python-jose, jsonwebtoken are popular libraries.

train.content: How to do API versioning?

API versioning allows updating the API without breaking existing users. Methods: URL versioning (/api/v1/users, /api/v2/users — most common, simplest), header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2), query parameter (?version=2). Semantic versioning: major (breaking change), minor (new feature), patch (bug fix). What's a breaking change: removing a field, renaming a field, changing response structure. Determine how long to support old versions (deprecation policy). Keep a changelog. Document each version with Swagger/OpenAPI. Good versioning builds user trust.

train.content: How to do web performance optimization?

Web performance directly affects user experience — Google also uses page speed as a ranking criterion. Core metrics: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint), FID (First Input Delay), CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) — Core Web Vitals. Optimization techniques: image compression (WebP format, lazy loading), CSS/JS minification, CDN usage, caching (browser cache, Redis), code splitting (only load needed JS), gzip/brotli compression, font optimization, prioritize above-the-fold content. Tools: Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights, WebPageTest. Set and track a performance budget.

train.content: How does SSL/TLS work?

SSL/TLS is the security protocol that encrypts internet connections — the S in HTTPS. TLS handshake: client connects to server → server sends certificate → client verifies → symmetric key is created → encrypted communication begins. Asymmetric encryption (public/private key) used in handshake, symmetric encryption for data transfer. SSL certificate: Let's Encrypt offers free certificates. Certificate Authority (CA) verifies certificates. HSTS header forces browsers to use HTTPS. HTTPS is mandatory in modern web — Google marks HTTP sites as insecure. Automate certificate renewal (certbot).
